chapter_title: Designing an A/B Test with Students
learning_objective: The learner will differentiate volunteer bias, convenience sampling, attrition, exclusion, and no concern by sorting each of six recruitment scenarios, with at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt.
specification:
Type: microsim **sim-id:** sampling-bias-spotter
**Library:** p5.js
**Status:** Specified
**Bloom Level:** Analyze
**Bloom Verb:** differentiate
**Learning Objective:** The learner will differentiate volunteer bias, convenience sampling, attrition, exclusion, and no concern by sorting each of six recruitment scenarios, with at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. **Prerequisites:** Sampling Bias, Sample Size, Treatment Group, Control Group (all defined in this chapter above this block). **Evidence of Mastery:** For each scenario the learner commits one of five bins. A placement is correct when it matches the Correct bin column in Content. Mastery is at least 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Reading the four forms is exploration, not evidence. **Misconceptions:** (1) Bias only occurs when the researcher is dishonest. (2) A volunteer is as good as a randomly chosen student. (3) Dropping students who did not finish is harmless. **Instructional Rationale:** Differentiating the forms of sampling bias is an Analyze-level action. Scenarios that each fail in one way, and two that are sound, teach the learner to ask who is missing and why. **Content:** The five bins: Volunteer bias, Convenience sampling, Attrition, Exclusion, No concern. The six scenarios (all made up): | # | Scenario | Correct bin | Why (shown as feedback) | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | A note is sent home, and only students who return a signed form take part. | Volunteer bias | Students who return forms tend to be more motivated. | | 2 | Only the teacher's honors class is tested, and the results are reported for all Grade 6 students. | Convenience sampling | One easy-to-reach class does not represent the grade. | | 3 | Nine students in the treatment group leave the test because the simulation would not load on their devices, and their scores are dropped. | Attrition | The students who remain are the ones whose devices worked. | | 4 | The improved version needs a laptop, so students without laptops are left out. | Exclusion | The test cannot speak for students who could not use it. | | 5 | Every student in the grade is invited, 24 of 25 in each section take part, and the reasons for the missing students are recorded. | No concern | Nearly everyone is included and the gaps are recorded. | | 6 | Three schools of different sizes are invited, and every student with consent takes part. | No concern | Participation does not depend on motivation or access. | **Provenance:** The scenarios are illustrative examples written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative examples". The four forms follow the chapter section "Sampling Bias". **Rules:** Each scenario has exactly one correct bin. Four scenarios have one of the four forms each, and two have no concern. **Learner Activity:** 1. The learner sees one scenario and the five bins, and may open the four forms. Opening them does not change the score. 2. The learner places the scenario in a bin, and the placement is committed. 3. The sim shows whether it was correct and the Why text. 4. After scenario 6 the sim shows the summary. **Feedback:** 6 scenarios in a shuffled order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [bin]. [Why]". Incorrect: "Not quite. This is [bin]. [Why]". The summary shows "[n] of 6 correct on the first attempt". At 5 or more it adds "You can spot who is missing from a test." Below 5 it lists the Why text of each missed scenario. **Starting State:** The first scenario in the shuffled order and the five bins. The question shown is "Who is missing, and why?" **Chapter Anchors:** The chapter lists four forms of sampling bias: volunteer bias, convenience sampling, attrition, and exclusion. The sim adds two cases with no concern.
